transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Celebrations in Baghdad is heard through the Associated Press now that the last American
troops have withdrawn from Iraq 23 years after the U.S. invasion.
At the White House today, President Trump noted that the U.S.'s military presence in
Iraq spanned the George W. Bush, Obama and Biden administrations but ended with his own.
Trump speaking today at a White House event celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month.
A flight from United Arab Emirates to Israel had to make an emergency landing after a pilot
allegedly tried to crash the plane with dozens of people on board.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says a pilot stabbed the co-pilot before being
neutralized by passengers and crew.
The fly-to-buy aircraft made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia before it continued
on to Israel.
The pilot has been arrested.
A group of small companies and nearly two dozen states are challenging President Trump's
latest effort to impose double-digit tariffs on nearly everything the U.S. imports.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the tariff opponents made their case before a specialized trade
court today.
After two earlier rounds of worldwide tariffs were struck down by the courts, the Trump
administration imposed a new set of import taxes, relying on a different trade law called
Section 301.
Plaintiff's lawyer Pratik Shah argues that law is designed to go after individual countries
that behave badly, not virtually every U.S. trading partner.
"It would be a massive transfer of taxing power from Congress to the executive to allow
them to forgo the country's specific sort of findings that 301 requires."
U.S. importers paid more than $20 billion in tariffs last month, but the government
also refunded $11 billion from earlier tariffs that were ruled illegal.
Scott Horsley, Impair News, Washington.
"A court has blocked Tennessee from carrying out the first execution of a woman in the
state for the first time in more than 200 years.
Judges are considering a defense motion about the woman's history of abuse as a child."
Tony Gonzalez of conversation WPLN reports.
Christa Pike was convicted for a murder she committed at age 18.
She and her boyfriend tortured and killed Knoxville classmate Colleen Slemmer.
Pike is 50 now and the only woman on death row in Tennessee.
Death penalty opponents have criticized the sentencing process.
It's in part because of how young Pike was when sentenced to death and how little court
consideration there was for her history of mental illness and severe childhood sexual
abuse.
Her defense team is also among those challenging the method of lethal injection.
Cases have mounted since a failed execution in May when medical staff couldn't insert
an IV.
That's Tony Gonzalez reporting.
This is NPR News.
The woman accused of firing a rifle at the home of Rihanna and A$AP Rocky has been charged.
An indictment unsealed today reveals that Ivana Lizette Ortiz has been charged with
multiple felonies including attempted murder.
She has pleaded not guilty.
Investigators allege Ortiz fired at least 20 rounds at the couple's home striking places
where the couple, their children and staff were located.
No injuries were reported.
The United Kingdom is advising all of its universities to cut ties with the China General
Technology Research Institute.
The government accuses the Chinese government of using the facility to develop spy technology.
Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, says more than 100 academics linked to the
UK have worked on projects secretly funded by Chinese intelligence.
It is illegal in the US to make a baby using gene-edited human embryos, but NPR's Rob Stein
explains at least two start-ups are hoping to change that.
Origin genomics in New York City and preventive bio in San Francisco are trying to produce
enough evidence to convince regulators that it would be safe to use modified embryos for
reproduction.
The companies say gene-editing embryos could help millions of babies from being born with
rare but devastating genetic disorders.
Critics, however, warn it may never be safe and worry that allowing gene-editing of human
embryos for any reason could open the door to someone trying to go further and create
designer babies.
Rob Stein, NPR News.

topics.text: Last American troops withdraw from Iraq after 23 years following U.S. invasion
President Trump notes U.S. military presence in Iraq ended during his administration
Pilot on United Arab Emirates flight to Israel attempts to crash plane, stabbed by crew
Aircraft makes emergency landing in Saudi Arabia before continuing to Israel, pilot arrested
Small companies and nearly two dozen states challenge Trump's double-digit import tariffs in court
Tennessee execution of woman blocked as judges consider her childhood abuse history
Christa Pike convicted of murder at age 18, now only woman on Tennessee death row
Woman Ivana Lizette Ortiz charged with attempted murder for firing at Rihanna and A$AP Rocky home
United Kingdom advises universities to cut ties with China General Technology Research Institute
Two U.S. startups seek regulatory approval to use gene-edited embryos for human reproduction
